title: Make a Bulb Light Up
subtitle: What a bulb really needs, and why two bulbs in a row shine dimmer than one. You are about to build the answer yourself.

sections.title: What does a bulb need?
sections.body:
Let’s try a little puzzle. Take a battery, a bulb and a piece of wire. Can you make the bulb glow? Most people try touching one end of the bulb to one end of the battery, and nothing happens. Don’t worry, that is not bad luck. It is the first big idea in electricity, and it is a good one.

A bulb only glows when electricity can travel all the way around and come back to where it started. That path is called a circuit, which is just a Latin-sounding word for “circle”. A circuit with a gap in it is called an open circuit, and an unbroken one is a closed circuit. Think of a toy train: it only runs if the track makes a full loop.

In this lesson you will build the circuit, open and close it, and then put in a second bulb to see what changes. Every picture on the page is a real, running experiment. Press Simulate on each one, and be curious!
keynotes: A bulb only glows when electricity can travel all the way around and come back to where it started.
That path is called a circuit: an open circuit has a gap, a closed circuit is unbroken.
Every picture is a real, running experiment: press Simulate.

sections.title: Your first closed circuit
sections.body:
Now we build it. Here is a battery, a switch, a bulb and a special meter called an ammeter. The ammeter counts how much electricity is flowing past it each second. That flow is called current, and we measure it in amperes (A) or in thousandths of an ampere, milliamperes (mA).

The switch is closed, so the loop is complete. Press Simulate and look at two things: the bulb, and the number on the ammeter. Did the bulb glow? The ammeter shows about 500 mA. Remember that number, because you will meet it again.

figures.caption: Figure 1.1 — a battery, a closed switch, a bulb and an ammeter
figures.note: Press Simulate. The bulb glows and the ammeter shows about 500 mA.

keynotes: An ammeter counts how much electricity flows past it each second.
That flow is called current, measured in amperes (A) or milliamperes (mA).
With the switch closed the bulb glows and the ammeter shows about 500 mA.

sections.title: What if the switch is open?
sections.body: Scientists make a guess before they look, and you can do the same. It is a great habit, because even a wrong guess teaches you something. Guess now, and then the experiment will show you who was right. What do you think happens when you open the switch and make a gap in the circuit?

questions.prompt: You open the switch, so there is a gap in the circuit. What happens to the bulb?

choices.text: It glows, but a little dimmer, because some electricity still leaks through.
It glows brighter, because the electricity is waiting at the gap.

responses.title: Nice thought, but there is no leak.
responses.body: A gap in a wire does not let a little electricity through. Air is an excellent insulator, so across a small gap the current is not "small", it is zero. The bulb is either in a complete loop or it is not.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: With a gap, nothing can flow around the loop, so the current is zero and the bulb is dark. This is exactly how a light switch on your wall works: it opens or closes a gap in the circuit.

responses.title: Electricity does not queue up.
responses.body: Charges only move when there is a complete path. A gap does not store the flow to release later. If one part of the loop cannot pass current, no part of the loop can, so the bulb gets nothing.

verify.caption: Check it — the same circuit with the switch open
verify.note: Press Simulate: the ammeter reads 0 and the bulb stays dark.

keynotes: Scientists make a guess before they look.
A wrong guess teaches you something too.
Opening the switch makes a gap in the circuit.

sections.title: Electricity is like water in a pipe
sections.body:
Electricity is invisible, so it helps to picture something you can see: a loop of pipe full of water, with a pump in it. The battery is the pump: it pushes. The wire is the pipe. The bulb is a narrow, rough section of pipe that is hard to push water through.

Now give the ideas their proper names. The push is called voltage (measured in volts, V). How hard the bulb makes it to flow is called resistance (measured in ohms, Ω). How much water flows past each second is the current. A stronger pump gives more flow. A narrower, rougher pipe gives less. Keep this picture in your head for the rest of the lesson.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2 — the pipe picture next to the real circuit words
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[Battery = the pump] as p #blue
[Wire = the pipe] as w #mint
[Bulb = a narrow pipe] as b #amber
[Current = water flowing each second] as c #violet
p -> w : pushes
w -> b
b -> c : sets how much
c -> p : comes back");

keynotes: In the pipe picture the battery is the pump, the wire is the pipe and the bulb is a narrow, rough section.
The push is voltage (volts, V); how hard the bulb makes it to flow is resistance (ohms, Ω); the flow is current.
A stronger pump gives more flow and a narrower, rougher pipe gives less.

sections.title: Two bulbs in a row
sections.body:
What happens if you add a second bulb? There are two ways to do it, and they behave very differently. First, put it in the same loop, right after the first. Electricity has one road only, and it must squeeze through both bulbs one after the other. This is called a series circuit.

Each bulb is the same, 12 Ω. Two of them in a row are harder to push current through than one, so the total resistance is 12 + 12 = 24 Ω. Press Simulate: the current is only 250 mA, half of Figure 1.1, so both bulbs shine dimmer. And if you unscrew one bulb in a series circuit, the loop is broken, so the other bulb goes out too.

figures.caption: Figure 1.3 — two bulbs in series
figures.note: Press Simulate: the current is only 250 mA, half of Figure 1.1, so both bulbs shine dimmer.

questions.prompt: In a series circuit, one of the two bulbs is unscrewed and removed. What happens to the other bulb?

choices.text: It stays lit, because it still has the battery.
It goes dark, because the loop now has a gap.

responses.title: The battery is not the only thing it needs.
responses.body: A bulb needs a complete loop, not just a battery. In a series circuit there is only one road, and the missing bulb leaves a gap in it, so no current flows to either bulb.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: In series there is only one path. Remove one bulb and you have opened the circuit, so every bulb goes dark. Old Christmas lights wired this way were famous for it: one dead bulb and the whole string went out.

responses.title: It would be nice, but no.
responses.body: Nothing speeds up when a bulb is removed. The current falls to zero, because the loop is broken, so the remaining bulb gets no current at all.

keynotes: In a series circuit electricity has one road only and must pass through both bulbs one after the other.
Two 12 Ω bulbs in series have a total resistance of 12 + 12 = 24 Ω.
The current is only 250 mA, half of Figure 1.1, so both bulbs shine dimmer.

sections.title: Two bulbs side by side
sections.body:
Here is the clever way to add a second bulb: give each bulb its own road straight to the battery. This is a parallel circuit. Each bulb gets the full push of the battery, so each shines as brightly as it would alone.

The battery now has two roads to send current down, so the total current doubles: 500 mA for each bulb makes 1000 mA, which is 1 A. Press Simulate and you will see the ammeter at the battery read about 1 A (999.8 mA), twice Figure 1.1. This is how the lights in your house are wired. Switch one off and the others stay on. Aren’t you glad?

figures.caption: Figure 1.4 — two bulbs in parallel
figures.note: Press Simulate: the ammeter at the battery reads about 1 A (999.8 mA), twice Figure 1.1.

keynotes: In a parallel circuit each bulb has its own road straight to the battery and gets the full push, so each shines as brightly as alone.
The total current doubles: 500 mA for each bulb makes 1000 mA, which is 1 A.
This is how the lights in your house are wired: switch one off and the others stay on.

sections.title: Working out the current
sections.body:
Now for the sum that ties it all together, and you can do it yourself. There is a rule that links the three ideas, and it is the most useful one in the whole chapter: current = voltage ÷ resistance. In letters, I = V ÷ R. This rule is called Ohm's law.

Follow along step by step below. The battery is 6 V and the bulb is 12 Ω, so I = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A, which is 500 mA. That is exactly what the ammeter showed in Figure 1.1! It reads 499.9 mA, a hair under, because real wires and batteries have a tiny resistance too. Physics predicted the experiment before you ran it.

worked.why: Write down what you know. The battery is 6 V and the bulb is 12 Ω.
Pick the rule that links them. We want current, so divide voltage by resistance.
Put the numbers in and do the division.

Check your answer against the experiment. 0.5 A is the same as 500 mA, which is what the ammeter in Figure 1.1 showed (it reads 499.9 mA, a hair under, because real wires and batteries have a tiny resistance too).

keynotes: Ohm's law links the three ideas: current = voltage ÷ resistance, or I = V ÷ R.
A 6 V battery and a 12 Ω bulb give I = 6 ÷ 12 = 0.5 A.
0.5 A is 500 mA, which matches the ammeter, a hair under at 499.9 mA.

sections.title: Try these

problems.prompt: A 9 V battery is connected to a 18 Ω bulb. How much current flows?
problems.answer: Divide voltage by resistance: 9 ÷ 18 = 0.5 A, which is 500 mA.

problems.prompt: Two 12 Ω bulbs are in series with a 6 V battery. What is the total resistance, and what current flows?
problems.answer: In series the resistances add: 12 + 12 = 24 Ω. Then 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25 A, or 250 mA, which is what Figure 1.3 shows.

verify.caption: Check it — two bulbs in series

problems.prompt: In your home, why are the lights wired in parallel and not in series?
problems.answer: In parallel each light gets the full voltage and works on its own, so one bulb failing or being switched off does not turn the others off. In series they would all depend on each other and all be dimmer.

sections.body: Now it is your turn. Work through these questions at your own pace: answer each one before you open its explanation, and use the experiments above to check yourself. If you get one wrong, don’t worry. That is exactly how you learn, and you can try again.

Use the experiments above to check yourself.
